units: the smell of the damp material strikes the visitor before anything else
a fine dust covers the floor of the room
the fast spinning of the wheel is the cause of this dust
unfired vessels are piled on the shelves
their grayish tone will change once they have been through the kiln
the presence of the kiln speeds up the drying of the pieces
the craftsman therefore protects certain pieces with a wet cloth
the walls have never been given any paint
every object set down in the workshop has a practical function
text: Push the workshop door open and the first thing that reaches you, before anything else, is the smell of wet clay. A fine dust lies across the whole floor, and the reason is the wheel: it scatters droplets in every direction the moment it picks up speed. Shelves sag under bowls that have not been fired yet, a dull gray that will turn warm brown once they come out of the kiln. The kiln sits at the back, and the heat it throws dries the pots far faster than anyone wants, so the potter keeps a damp cloth draped over the ones he is not touching. The walls are rough and have never seen a coat of paint, so they hold the dust instead of shedding it. Stay an hour and you understand that nothing here is decorative. Every tool on the bench does one particular job, and the order you think you see comes out of use, not out of tidiness.

units: the closing of a venue happens in successive stages
the usual explanation blames the public for losing interest
the crowds at nearby stages contradict this explanation
the level of the rent swallows the margin of the takings
a first solution is to share technical costs between venues
these venues wrongly consider one another as rivals
a second solution rests on long leases
this guarantee demands affordable prices and original creations given a stage in return
text: A theater rarely closes all at once. It dims in stages: a season trimmed, a subscription put on hold, a technical crew cut back. The standard verdict blames audiences for drifting away, yet the lines outside the halls down the street make that verdict look lazy. What actually squeezes these houses is rent, which swallows whatever margin the box office still produces. Two remedies exist, and neither one calls for a miracle. The first is to pool the heavy costs, the sets, the lighting boards, the insurance, among venues that treat one another as rivals while courting the very same audience. The second is to lock in long leases, tied to something firm in return: seats people can afford and original creations given a stage. Otherwise we will go on mourning closures we arranged ourselves.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a specialist repairs old paintings
her manner recalls that of a repairer of watches
both trades call for tiny movements repeated over and over
she lifts the darkened varnish with a swab of cotton
she halts her hand as soon as the tone underneath looks doubtful
the material of a movement responds in a predictable way
a painting instead puts up old touch-ups and deposits of smoke
the aim of the repairer of watches is to get the object running again
the aim of the specialist is to keep the painter's gesture readable
text: The painting restorer bends over a canvas the way a watchmaker bends over a stopped movement. For both of them the motions are tiny and endlessly repeated, and a slip forgives nothing. She lifts yellowed varnish in patches no wider than a fingernail, with cotton rolled onto a slim stick, and she stops her hand the moment the color underneath looks uncertain. The watchmaker straightens a toothed wheel that a knock has bent, and metal answers her plainly, while paint answers with buried changes of mind, with old touch-ups, with layers grimed by lamp smoke. The difference lies in the aim. The watchmaker wants the machine running again. The restorer wants nothing running at all. She only wants some later eye to still read what a hand laid down there, one evening, on stretched cloth.

units: the exhibition shows prints
the deep inks do not clog the dark areas
the paper used has a grainy texture
this texture softens the contrast of the light areas
the order of hanging follows the successive states of the plates
this arrangement makes the progress of the engraved drawing visible
the labels lack any indication of the technique used
this absence leaves the uninformed visitor at a loss
text: Three things go right in this hanging of prints, and one thing goes wrong. Start with the inking: the blacks stay dense without ever filling the hollows, which lets the finest lines breathe and gives some sheets a startling depth. Then the support, a coarse-grained paper that feels almost felted under a fingertip and takes the edge off the whites, so the contrast never turns harsh. Then the sequence, since the plates hang by successive states and a visitor watches the image assemble itself, from a half-finished sketch to the final pull. What goes wrong is the labeling, silent about the process, the tool, the bite of the acid. Anyone who already knows the craft can piece it together alone. Anyone meeting it for the first time leaves with a vague admiration and nothing learned.

units: the writer thanks the woman who led an engraving course
he came to the studio with no earlier experience
the first session dealt with preparing the plates
he then learned to control how long the bite lasts
one of his plates was ruined during the attempt
the woman in charge offered to let him start again right away
the last session yielded a successful pull
the writer wishes to enroll in the following course
text: I am writing at the close of the engraving course you led, and I want to thank you for it. I came to the studio with no practice whatever, uneasy about holding a needle in front of people who plainly knew what they were doing. The opening session, given over to degreasing and grounding the plates, put that worry to rest. Your instructions were plain and exact, and nobody in the room was left behind. We moved on to controlling the bite, and I understood that the time spent in the bath decides nearly everything. My second plate was ruined by too long a soak, and you told me at once to prepare another, without a word of reproach. The last session produced a clean pull that I am proud of. So I would very much like to enroll in the course that follows, if there are any places still left.

units: a technician explains how old recordings are brought back
the hiss comes from the wearing down of the original medium
filtering too hard also wipes out useful sound
the high end of the string instruments goes first
the technician therefore prefers a measured correction
he compares several copies of the same recording
this comparison tells a flaw in one copy from a flaw shared by all
he always keeps an unaltered version of the file
text: People keep asking the sound technician where that haze over old recordings actually comes from. His answer is a short one: the medium wore down, and wear lays a steady hiss over everything, a hiss the microphone never picked up. Can it be wiped away for good? No, he says, and it should not be, because heavy filtering carries off the topmost overtones of the strings along with the noise, and what is left sounds dull. What does he do instead? He applies a restrained correction, then sets several copies of the same disc side by side. A crackle on one copy belongs to that copy. A crackle on all of them belongs to the cutting itself. One rule governs the whole job: the original stays archived untouched, because a listening choice that felt right yesterday can look wrong tomorrow.

units: an actress tells a stage manager about a sound problem
her voice cannot be made out at the back of the hall
the stage manager first assumes the microphone is failing
the wooden set is in fact throwing the sound back toward the stage
a thick rug is laid on the floor to soak up the reflections
the speakers are turned toward the far seats
the actress checks the result from the last row
the trouble is gone by the next rehearsal
text: The actress caught the stage manager at the edge of the platform and told him that nobody past the third row could make out a single word she said. He figured the microphone was going flat, and said he would swap the battery out and see what happened. She pushed back. The trouble started earlier than that, before the mic ever got involved, because the plank set was throwing her own voice straight back at her and pushing her to shove harder. He granted she was right, then suggested a heavy rug at the foot of the panel to soak up those returns. After that they tilted the speakers toward the far rows, which had been sitting in a dead patch. She went back there to listen while an understudy read her lines, and came up saying it was clear at last. At the next run, nobody craned forward.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two old ways of fixing images are set against each other
wall painting addresses a large audience
the decorated manuscript is meant for a single reader
wall painting is carried out quickly on plaster that is still damp
the illuminator can break off and take up the work again at will
wall painting suffered from changes in what the buildings were used for
manuscripts came through better because they were stored out of harm's way
the two techniques used comparable pigments
text: Two ways of fixing an image lived side by side for a long while, and they disagree about almost everything. Painting on a wall speaks to a crowd. It takes a whole surface, reads from a distance, and forces its figures on anyone who steps through the door. A decorated page speaks to one reader, alone and stooped, turning leaves at whatever pace suits him. Part of the gap comes from the craft itself. Damp plaster gives the painter one working stretch and no more, which rules out second thoughts and demands a sure hand, while the illuminator shuts his volume and takes it up whenever he likes. Their fates parted as well. Walls were whitewashed, cut through and put to other uses as the buildings changed, while volumes shut in a cupboard came through whole. The pigments, though, were ground from the same stuff.

units: the colorants used in painting come from three distinct sources
the first source is mineral and comes from crushed rock
these mineral powders hold their tone for a long time
the second source is vegetable and comes from roots or berries
vegetable colorants fade under a bright light
the third source comes from insects or shells
these last ones were scarce and expensive
a binder turns the colored powder into a paste that can be used
text: Three families of color share the painter's palette, and each one of them carries a tale of where it came from. The first comes out of stone. Crush a pebble, sift the powder, and down falls a deep blue or a warm ocher that will hold its note for ages, since rock keeps no memory of the light thrown on it. The second is born of plants, of roots torn up, of berries crushed, of wood left to steep, and those tints are airy, almost afloat, lovely at first sight, yet they pale under a strong light and end up shadows of themselves. The third comes from living creatures, from gathered shells and dried insects, and its scarcity kept it for lavish commissions. One gesture runs through all three: powder is nothing until a binder takes hold of it and turns it into a paste that can be worked.

units: a tuner works on an instrument before a concert
the hall was too warm when he arrived
the heat had slackened the strings unevenly
he first set a reference note against the tuning fork
he then adjusted the other notes by successive fifths
a bass string gave way during the operation
he replaced that string and then stretched it by hand
he measured the temperature before checking a second time
text: The tuner walked into the hall a good hour before the concert, and he knew from the doorway that the air in there was far too warm. The heat had slackened the stringing unevenly, the bass having drifted further than the middle register. He began by setting a reference note against the fork, by ear, with no device at all, then climbed in fifths, narrowing each interval by a beat he counted off. The work turned rough. On the third pass a bass string gave way outright and the wire coiled itself onto the soundboard. He fitted a fresh one, seated it firmly on its pin, and pulled it by hand so it would settle before the players showed up. Then, with a thermometer in his palm, he waited for the air to drop and then took the whole instrument through again, starting over from the very first note.
